field_key.q: How many independent channels reach it?
field_key.a: Many for its acts: the Federal Register, court dockets, contracts, a rival's foreign ministry and the press. For its premise, that the leader will set the world's terms, none yet: it is a forecast, and its holders disagree on what serves it.

Nearest outside: the rival's government, which calls for “global solidarity” while, Reuters reports, restricting H200 imports; the MAIM authors, who propose deterrence instead of a bid for monopoly while still urging competitiveness; FLI, critics writing in Lawfare, Pope Leo XIV, and twenty countries and the EU (September 2026, in Al Jazeera's count; FLI counts 22 countries); and the courts, which have ruled both ways on Anthropic. cautions: Anthropic is on both sides of this ideal. Its chief executive states it (“to defeat our autocratic adversaries”, February 2026) and in September 2026 asked to slow AI capabilities while keeping the democracies' lead “as large as possible”; the President answered, NPR reports, that “whoever wins AI, wins”. It is criticised from inside the race camp: David Sacks wrote on X, as TechCrunch shows, “Anthropic is running a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering.” (his accusation; Anthropic answered what it called “inaccurate claims”), and an Nvidia spokesperson said “America cannot manipulate regulators to capture victory in AI” (NBC News). After it refused two uses, the Department designated it a supply chain risk, and its model is reported to be part of the Maven targeting system used in the Iran war. Anthropic's own figures on forgone revenue and losses were not checked. This map is made with Anthropic's models, and Anthropic is a party here.

The label is this map's; its carriers' own word is the race. That the leader will set the world's terms and hold a decisive advantage is a forecast in its holders' words (Aschenbrenner, the Action Plan, Amodei), not a finding, and so are the dates attached to it, such as Aschenbrenner's government AGI project “by 27/28”. “Super Intelligence” in US federal documents since September 2026 is a new name for AI under an executive order, not evidence that superintelligence exists. This map is made with Anthropic's models, and Anthropic is a party here.

Its holders differ on what serves it: in January 2026 the administration opened H200-class chip exports to China to case-by-case licensing, citing “U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence”; Amodei called shipping them “a big mistake”, The Register reports; and Nvidia wrote in January 2025, against an earlier export rule, that America wins “by sharing our technologies with the world”. China's stated position sits beside its own moves in the contest: it calls for “global solidarity” while, Reuters reports, restricting H200 imports “as it seeks to reduce its dependence on US technology”. The map records each and rules on none. This map is made with Anthropic's models, and Anthropic is a party here.

The two court results on Anthropic rest on different statutes, and a Taft law bulletin says they “are not in conflict”. On retaliation they reached opposite conclusions: the district court declared the measures “unlawful retaliation”, while the D.C. Circuit majority, as Taft summarises it, held that Anthropic was removed for refusing the department's contract terms, not for its advocacy. Both are under further review, and neither decides whether Anthropic's limits or the military's demand were wise. This map is made with Anthropic's models, and Anthropic is a party here.

The race is invoked on both sides of the Anthropic dispute. The Pentagon said “The military will not allow a vendor to insert itself into the chain of command by restricting the lawful use of a critical capability” (AP), and the government's brief cites “the risk that petitioner may unilaterally manipulate its software to enforce its own moral and policy judgments about the military’s appropriate use”. Anthropic said “No amount of intimidation or punishment from the Department of War will change our position on mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons.”, and the Foundation for American Innovation, whose senior fellow Dean Ball it says helped draft the Action Plan, argued “Blacklisting Anthropic Weakens U.S. AI Leadership”. The stated scope of the penalty changed between the Secretary's post and the government's brief three weeks later; the map does not say which reading governs. This map is made with Anthropic's models, and Anthropic is a party here.

Accounts of Claude's role in the Maven Smart System differ: Military Times says it is used “to semi-autonomously rank targets by strategic importance”; Semafor says it “quickly scans and summarizes relevant documents”; an analyst in Defense One says “Claude does not directly provide targeting recommendations”. On the Minab school strike, death tolls differ by source (from more than 150 to 175 killed); Semafor's sources blame human error, not AI, while ThePrint, relaying Bloomberg, reports that officials in the Pentagon's internal review described a “cascade of preventable failures”, among them outdated satellite imagery and personnel “over-relying on and over-trusting” Maven. No source read establishes what Claude did in that targeting, and the Pentagon's investigation has not been published. This map is made with Anthropic's models, and Anthropic is a party here.

Money ties run through it, and none is a finding about motive. Aschenbrenner's fund, Situational Awareness LP, kept a stake in Anthropic as its largest private holding, TechCrunch reports (July 2026); Anthropic held one of the four $200 million-ceiling Pentagon awards; the Special Competitive Studies Project calls itself a subsidiary of Eric and Wendy Schmidt's operating foundation, and Eric Schmidt co-wrote Superintelligence Strategy, which argues against a US Manhattan Project. This map is made with Anthropic's models, and Anthropic is a party here.

The old texts set beside this ideal are this project's reading: none is about AI, and none proves anything about who will lead in AI.
